title: Selectors and Specificity
description: Target DOM elements with type, class, ID, attribute, and combinator selectors, and calculate CSS specificity weights (Inline > ID > Class/Attribute > Element) to resolve conflicting styles.

objectives.statement: Target elements accurately using element, class, ID, and descendant selectors.
Calculate selector specificity to predict winning styles when multiple rules compete.

content.title: Precision Targeting & Specificity Rules
content.hook: When multiple CSS rules target the exact same element with conflicting properties, which one wins? CSS resolves this deterministically using Specificity.
content.context: Selectors have different weights: Element selectors (0,0,1), Class/Attribute selectors (0,1,0), and ID selectors (1,0,0). The most specific rule wins regardless of order in the file.
goals: Target elements with class, ID, and descendant combinators (`nav a`).
Avoid specificity wars and over-specified selectors.

content.title: The CSS Specificity Weight Matrix
content.description: Comparison of selector weights: Element `p` (0,0,1) vs Class `.card` (0,1,0) vs Class+Element `div.card` (0,1,1) vs ID `#hero` (1,0,0). Higher category wins.

content.prompt: Given the HTML `<button id="main-btn" class="btn primary">Click</button>`, which color is applied to the button?
options: blue (because Rule A has three selectors)
green (because Rule C appears last in the stylesheet)
red (because the ID selector #main-btn has higher specificity weight (1,0,0) than classes or elements)
black (browser default because conflicting rules cancel each other out)

validation.expected: red (because the ID selector #main-btn has higher specificity weight (1,0,0) than classes or elements)

feedback.correct: Exactly! `#main-btn` has specificity (1,0,0), which beats `button.btn.primary` (0,2,1). A single ID selector always trumps any number of classes or elements.
feedback.incorrect: Calculate the specificity matrix: ID column takes precedence over Class column. `#main-btn` is (1,0,0), while `button.btn.primary` is (0,2,1). Red wins.

content.title: Target Elements with Precision Selectors
content.prompt:
Write CSS rules to style the components:
1. Target the `.highlight` class and give it `background-color: yellow`.
2. Target anchor tags inside the navigation (`nav a`) and give them `color: #0284c7`.
3. Target the button with `id="cta-btn"` and give it `background-color: #10b981` and `color: #ffffff`.

testCases.description: .highlight must have background-color of yellow / rgb(255, 255, 0)
nav a links must have color of #0284c7 / rgb(2, 132, 199)
#cta-btn must have green background (#10b981 / rgb(16, 185, 129)) and white text

feedback.correct: Excellent selector craftsmanship! You used class, descendant, and ID selectors with accurate precision.
feedback.incorrect: Verify your selector syntax: `.highlight` for classes, `nav a` for descendant links, and `#cta-btn` for IDs.

hints.content: Use `.highlight { background-color: yellow; }` for the class selector.
Use `nav a { color: #0284c7; }` to target links inside the nav element.

content.prompt: Why do professional frontend architectures (like BEM or utility CSS) avoid using ID selectors for styling in favor of classes?

feedback.correct: Great insight! ID selectors carry such high specificity (1,0,0) that they create brittle stylesheets where rules cannot easily be overridden or reused across multiple components without escalating specificity wars.
feedback.incorrect: Consider reusability (IDs must be unique) and specificity wars (IDs are very hard to override).

content.title: Key Takeaways: Selectors & Specificity
takeaways: Element selectors match tag names (p, h1, div).
Class selectors (.name) match class attributes and are the foundation of scalable CSS.
ID selectors (#id) match unique elements but have high specificity that can cause maintenance issues.
Descendant selectors (parent child) match nested elements at any depth.
